claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(a) and 10(b)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: Classification runs by category, and publication is the exception. Section 10(b)(1): restricted data 'means all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.' Section 10(a) makes it 'the policy of the Commission to control the dissemination of restricted data in such a manner as to assure the common defense and security.'

The military keeps a standing claim over the control of weapons information, with an appeal that ends at the President. Section 2(c) directs that the Commission 'shall advise and consult with the Committee on all atomic energy matters which the Committee deems to relate to military applications, including the development, manufacture, use, and storage of bombs, the allocation of fissionable material for military research, and the control of information relating to the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons', and provides that where either Secretary concurs in a Military Liaison Committee objection he 'may refer the matter to the President, whose decision shall be final.'

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(4), and identically at 10(b)(2)(A) and 10(b)(3), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The penalty reaches concealment and destruction, not only disclosure, and it is capital. Section 10(b)(4) provides that whoever 'removes, conceals, tampers with, alters, mutilates, or destroys' a document incorporating restricted data with intent to injure the United States 'shall be punished by death or imprisonment for life (but the penalty of death or imprisonment for life may be imposed only upon recommendation of the jury and only in cases where the offense was committed with intent to injure the United States); or by a fine of not more than $20,000 or imprisonment for not more than twenty years, or both.'

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 21 and chapter head, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The Act's own short title is narrow: 'This Act may be cited as the "Atomic Energy Act of 1946".' The chapter head gives it as Chapter 724, S. 1717, Public Law 585, 79th Congress, 'AN ACT For the development and control of atomic energy', approved August 1, 1946. The popular name 'McMahon Act' appears nowhere in the statute.

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(5)(B)(i) and 10(b)(5)(C), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The FBI is both the gate and the investigator. Section 10(b)(5)(B)(i) bars any arrangement, contract or licence unless the contractor 'agrees in writing not to permit any individual to have access to restricted data until the Federal Bureau of Investigation shall have made an investigation and report to the Commission on the character, associations, and loyalty of such individual.' Section 10(b)(5)(C): 'All violations of this Act shall be investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation of the Department of Justice.'

claims.nodeLabel: Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (Pub. L. 83-703, 68 Stat. 919)
claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1954 secs. 11 r. and 141-145 against Atomic Energy Act of 1946 sec. 10, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-68/pdf/STATUTE-68-Pg919.pdf and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: WHAT CHANGED FROM 1946, FROM THE TWO TEXTS SIDE BY SIDE. The 1946 Act defined 'restricted data' only 'as used in this section', at section 10; the 1954 Act makes 'Restricted Data' a capitalised, Act-wide definition in the definitions chapter. 1954 ADDS the word 'design'. 'Fissionable material' and 'production of power' become 'special nuclear material' and 'production of energy'. And the 1946 carve-out was open-ended Commission discretion, where 1954 ties removal to a formal declassification procedure at section 142, including the transclassification of weapons-utilisation data into 'defense information' under section 142 d.

claims.nodeLabel: Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (Pub. L. 83-703, 68 Stat. 919)
claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946 sec. 10(b)(1), 60 Stat. 755, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The 1946 definition it replaced, at section 10(b)(1), covered 'all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power'.

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 9(a), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The Commission took statutory custody of the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings. Section 9(a) directs the transfer to the Commission of 'All fissionable material; all atomic weapons and parts thereof' and of 'Such other property owned by or in the custody or control of the Manhattan Engineer District or other Government agencies as the President may determine.'

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 10(b)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: Classification runs by category rather than by decision. The 1946 Act defines restricted data as 'all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.'

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 2(a), approved 1 August 1946, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf
claims.text: The Commission was created by statute: 'There is hereby established an Atomic Energy Commission (herein called the Commission), which shall be composed of five members.' Members are appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.

claims.sourceText: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 2(a)(4)(B), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf ; Atomic Energy Act of 1954, Public Law 83-703, 68 Stat. 919, sec. 25, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-68/pdf/STATUTE-68-Pg919.pdf
claims.text: A Division of Military Application under a serving officer was in the Commission from the start: the 1946 Act establishes it alongside Research, Production and Engineering and provides that 'The Director of the Division of Military Application shall be a member of the armed forces.' The 1954 Act carries it forward at section 25 with the Director required to be 'an active member of the Armed Forces.'

edges.label: Statutory transfer of the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings and its cleared people
edges.note: Section 9(a) directs the transfer of all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts and all processes and technical information, and section 10(b)(5)(B)(iii) lets anyone the Manhattan Engineer District had already cleared keep access pending the new investigation.

edges.label: The instrument that created the Commission
edges.note: Section 2(a) of this Act establishes the Atomic Energy Commission and section 10 gives it the born-secret regime the Commission then ran for twenty-eight years.

a.label: Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (Pub. L. 83-703, 68 Stat. 919)

edges.label: Restates the 1946 Act rather than repealing it, and widens the definition
edges.note: The long title is 'To amend the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, as amended, and for other purposes'. The definition moves from a section-only usage to an Act-wide capitalised category, gains the word 'design', and swaps fissionable material and power for special nuclear material and energy.

edges.label: Statutory transfer of the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings
edges.note: Section 9(a) of the 1946 Act directs the President to transfer to the Commission all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts, all processes and technical information, and such other property in the custody or control of the Manhattan Engineer District as he may determine.
